vignette:
He sits across from me, hands folded tightly in his lap, the knuckles pale. His posture is precise, almost rigid—the same way he describes arranging columns of figures in his tax consultancy office. He tells me he has been having trouble sleeping, but that’s not why he came. His wife made the appointment. She told him he’s “not the same person” she married. When he says this, his jaw tightens, and he looks past me, toward the window, as if searching for an exit.

He was twenty-nine when he volunteered as a relief worker with an international NGO. It was a three-month deployment to a war-torn region in the Middle East. He had just passed his CPA exam, felt restless, wanted to do something meaningful before settling into a career. He describes the first weeks as a blur of dust, heat, and the constant low thrum of generators. He worked in a field hospital, handling logistics—supplies, transport, paperwork. Numbers, he says, were his refuge.

Then came the airstrike. He was in the storage tent, counting boxes of IV bags. The ground shook. The lights went out. He heard screams, then a child’s voice calling for her mother. He ran outside. The main clinic was gone. He helped carry the wounded for hours. He remembers a girl, maybe seven, her leg crushed. He held her hand while a doctor amputated. She stopped crying at some point. He doesn’t remember the rest of that night, only the wet warmth of her small fingers in his.

When he returned home, he tried to go back to his old life. But the numbers didn’t feel safe anymore. Now, when he reviews a client’s tax return, he sometimes sees the girl’s face in the columns of figures. He blinks, and she’s gone. He tells himself it’s just stress, fatigue. He starts staying late at the office, working weekends. His wife asks why. He says he’s busy. The truth is, he can’t bear the quiet of home. The silence reminds him of the stillness after the airstrike, when the only sound was his own breathing.

He avoids restaurants that serve Middle Eastern food. The smell of cumin or cardamom makes his stomach clench. He flinches when a car backfires on the street. He drives the long way to avoid a construction site where a jackhammer sounds like a mortar. His wife tries to hold his hand; he pulls away without thinking. He feels guilty about that, but he can’t explain why his skin crawls.

He has nightmares most nights—the girl’s face, the dust, the darkness. Sometimes he wakes up already on his feet, heart pounding, searching for an exit in his own bedroom. He hasn’t told anyone this. Not his wife, not his doctor. He came to therapy only because she threatened to leave. He says he’s fine—his work is fine, his clients are fine. But his hands are still in his lap, and he hasn’t let go of his grip the entire hour.

When I ask what he hopes to get from coming here, he is quiet for a long time. Then he says, very softly, “I just want to stop seeing her.” He doesn’t mean his wife. He means the girl. He means the piece of himself he left in that tent.
